## Abstract

## Motivation

The culinary arts are a complex subject area and an interesting area of potential optimization. It is a difficult domain to model with data due to its many hard-to-measure features, such as the wide range of ingredients, the specificity of heat and time measurements, the various techniques and steps, and the evaluation of the results. Culinary dishes often do not present well as an optimization problem, as maximizing taste or texture, for example, is not objective. As such, there is little applied data science in the domain outside of the privte commercial food industry.

One sub-domain that circumvents some of these issues is baking. Many baking recipes involve a small list of ingredients, as few as four in many cases - salt, water, flour, and yeast. Additionally, it is quite common to represent these (and any other ingredients) as "baker's percentages", as a percentage of the amount of flour used. These formulations solve the aforementioned specificity and measurement problems. Unfortunately, if we are interested in optimizing these formulations towards a specific outcome, we must be able to describe and label such outcomes (as classes) consistently. For baking broadly, this is not feasible due to the very large number of potential classes. For this reason, we are specifically interested in pizza dough formulations.

Pizza needs no introduction; it is one of the most widely recognized and popular foods in the world, with many distinct regional variations, a small and economical ingredient list, and a relatively straightforward product for both consumer and commercial sectors. 

In particular, consumer interest in at-home pizza making has grown rapidly. Manufacturers specializing in dedicated pizza equipment, such as Ooni and Gozney, have seen remarkable market growth. Gozney Group Limited's filed UK accounts show turnover rising from £12.9M in the financial year ended 31 March 2021 to £60.7M in the year ended 31 March 2024 - four consecutive years of compounding growth, at +111%, +62%, and +37% respectively.[^gozney] Its closest competitor, Ooni, is reported to have reached roughly $200M in annual revenue at its peak, easing to approximately $194M in 2023 as pandemic-era demand normalized.[^ooni]

Interest in recipes for specific styles has also increased. Among the rising US pizza dough queries of the five years to September 2026, four of the fifteen highest-volume are Neapolitan-specific: "neapolitan pizza dough recipe" and "neapolitan pizza" both carry a search-interest index of 24, and "neapolitan pizza dough" and "neapolitan pizza recipe" both carry 23.[^trends] This indicates real consumer interest in the formulation of specific pizza dough styles.

![The fifteen highest-volume rising US pizza dough search queries, September 2021 - September 2026](../../figures/pizza_dough_rising_queries_light.svg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

As such, this paper explores culinary optimization, using pizza a sub-domain, as a machine learning problem, focused on guiding and optimizing pizza dough formulae development. Our goal is to explore the feasibility of using statistical methods and machine learning to classify three popular pizza styles (Neapolitan, New York, and Sicillian) from dough formula, and allow for more efficient development than trial and error.

<### Managing Consumer Home Making Variables>

This framework in particular supports the consumer who cooks and develops recipes at home, an environment with a much larger range of variables, including;

- Oven temperatures & thermostat accuracy
- Imprecise volume measurements
- Inconsistenty & availability of ingredients
- Limited resources for large volumes of samples
- Environmental differences, including altitude and humidity
- Limited resources 

These types of variables are difficult control, especially from user to user. As such, we propose that dough formulation is the best tool available to a home cook to achieve a particular outcome. As the data for these factors are not available, we can attempt to normalize them and provide the means for a user to fine-tune a formula to their specific environmental factors.

<### Additional Applications to Commercial Users>

This is not to say the implications are limited to home users. Commercial users may find it useful for product development, no-cost experimentation, and scaling to their particular operations. For example, a pizzeria that specializes in Neapolitan pizzas made with a particular local flour may wish to explore a New York style offering. They would likely wish to differentiate their products sufficiently, while still using the same local flour. Having the ability to take their base recipe and adjust towards a new distinct offering, while keeping their preferred ingredient list, can reduce experimentation cyles and matertial costs.

In short, we expect that our methods could be useful to a wide range of formula developers across sectors.

## Background of dough formulation

We have focused much on the dough formulation thus far, ignoring other ingredients, proofing times, shaping techniques, and firing temperatures. While these are certaintly interesting features, it is beyond our scope to attempt to encode each of these factors in a standardized way.

As mentioned before, baking perccentages are numerical features of a dough formla, allowing us a consistent vector representation expressed as;

$$
r = \big(\mathbf{p},\ t_{\text{flour}},\ t_{\text{yeast}},\ t_{\text{fat}},\ t_{\text{sugar}}\big)
$$ {#eq-recipe}

Here $\mathbf{p}$ holds the baker's percentages. For each ingredient $i \in \mathcal{I} = \{\text{flour}, \text{water}, \text{salt}, \text{yeast}, \text{fat}, \text{sugar}\}$ with mass $m_i$ in grams, the baker's percentage is its mass relative to the flour:

$$
p_i = 100 \cdot \frac{m_i}{m_{\text{flour}}}
$$ {#eq-bakers}

Flour is therefore always $p_{\text{flour}} = 100$. A constant carries no information, so it is left out, and the remaining five ratios form

$$
\mathbf{p} = (p_{\text{water}},\ p_{\text{salt}},\ p_{\text{yeast}},\ p_{\text{fat}},\ p_{\text{sugar}}) \in \mathbb{R}^5_{\ge 0}.
$$

Each ingredient $i \in \mathcal{K} = \{\text{flour}, \text{yeast}, \text{fat}, \text{sugar}\}$ also has a type $t_i$, drawn from a fixed vocabulary $\mathcal{T}_i$. For example, $\mathcal{T}_{\text{flour}} = \{\text{all-purpose}, \text{bread}, \text{double zero}, \text{high-gluten}, \text{semolina}\}$. The notation used throughout is collected in @tbl-notation.

This is a natural representation for dough formulas; baking percentages are captured as numerica features, while the classes of these ingredients, such as high-fluten or all-purpose flours, is encoded as categorical. These are the core features that are present in every formula.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-worked-example
# TABLE: worked example of one corpus recipe, e.g. neapolitan_001.
# Columns: ingredient | grams as published | baker's % (@eq-bakers) | type.
# Shows the raw recipe -> r = (p, t) representation of @eq-recipe concretely.
```

We have allowed for common dough enrichments, including fat such as olive oil, and sugars such as refined white sugar. The presence or absence of these optional ingedients can contain valuable information as to the culinary style of the formula.

An absent enrichment has both a zero ratio and the type $\text{none}$, and the two always go together:

$$
p_i = 0 \iff t_i = \text{none}, \qquad i \in \{\text{fat}, \text{sugar}\}
$$

### Pizza Styles

We have briefly mentioned a few pizza styles thus far. Due to the limitation of data, and popularity of the following styles, we have limited our study to Neapolitan, New York, and Sicillian.

Neapolitan is the most clearly defined style of pizza. Originating from Naples, Italy, it is characterized by a soft, pillowy, unenriched dough. Usually smaller than other styles, the base of the crust is thin, with a highly aerated perimiter. Neapolitan pizza is defined very clearly by the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (AVPN) Internal Regulations, however in keeping with other styles, this was not used as a definitive centroid (although it is one of the recipes). Neapolitan pizzas are typically baked in extremely hot specific ovens, fueled by hardwoods.

New York Style is another well known style originating in New York City, where it is often served as an affordable street food by the slice. These pies are typically much larger and thinner than other styles, with a crisp even crust, baked in commercial ovens.

Sicillian is not quite as well known, but we've chosen it as many other popular styles, including Detroit, are very similar. It also provides a point of contrast to the other two styles - Sicillian pizza uses a much thicker dough than either New York or Neapolitan, and is generally a much more approachable style of pizza to the consumer sector as it does not require such extreme baking temperatures or dough handling technique.

There are of course many other styles of pizza, but these are well known and typically recognized by their dough more so than other styles.


## Data

Labeled pizza formulations are not readily available as structured data. As such, we have developed a small, well-structured dataset of expert-curated recipes. By focusing on expert recipes, we can establish clear profiles of each pizza style against which to measure other formulations. Imposing constraints will allow us to be confident in our class labels,

We followed the below criteria for identifying expert recipes;

- Published on official company websites relevant to the domain, such as Gozney, Ooni, and King Arthur
- Authored by culinarians highly regarded and recognized in their industry, including James Beard award winners Kenji Alt-Lopez, Chris Young, and Ken Forkish
- Popular recipes in pizza-focused online communities and forms, such as pizza-making.com. Popularity was inferred from the presence of a "stickied" forum post, posts provided by community leaders, or other high-traffic content with community acclaim.
- Recipes expressed in baker's percentages published on independent websites operated by pizza restaurantours

<### Data Collection>

Formulations for our targeted styles were gathered ethically, following site scraping rules and requirements. Most recipes were gathered by hand as raw text.

The dough formulation portion of the recipe was then extracted and structured in a common schema. Conversions and normalization of the data was performed deterministically in code. 

<### Data Processing>

Recipes were processed by converting nominal measurements of flour, water, salt, and yeast into baker's percentages.

Each ingredient mass was divided by the flour mass as in @eq-bakers. When a formula blends several flours, $m_{\text{flour}}$ is their combined mass.

Flour, water, salt, and yeast types were assigned a default value if not specified. Types were normalized to a finite list of options based on our domain knowledge. For example, King Arthur Sir Lancelot is a relatively high-gluten flour product, and as such would be assigned a "high gluten" flour type.

Sourdough starters, poolishes, or other developed bacterial colonies were converted into respective water, flour, and yeast quantities following expert heuristics.

Volume measurements are a common source of inconsistency - these were first converted to metric measurements by expert guided conversions before then computing the remaining vector quantities. Note that formulas using volume measurements are imprecise by nature, and this convention will bias these formulas.

## Feature Space

We define here our feature space. 

Each formula is mapped to a feature vector $\mathbf{x} = \phi(r) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ in two steps: the ratios in $\mathbf{p}$ are standardized, and the ingredient types are one-hot encoded.

**Scaling.** The ingredients sit on very different scales. Water ranges from about 57 to 75%, while yeast ranges from about 0.06 to 1.5%. Yet a 0.5-point change in yeast or salt changes the dough far more than a 0.5-point change in hydration. Unscaled distances would be dominated by water, and as such, each ratio in $\mathbf{p}$ is therefore standardized against the reference corpus $\mathcal{D}$, writing $p_i^{(r)}$ for the ratio of ingredient $i$ in recipe $r$:

$$
z_i = \frac{p_i - \mu_i}{\sigma_i}, \qquad
\mu_i = \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{D}} p_i^{(r)}, \qquad
\sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{D}} \big(p_i^{(r)} - \mu_i\big)^2
$$ {#eq-zscore}

This gives $\mathbf{z} = (z_{\text{water}}, z_{\text{salt}}, z_{\text{yeast}}, z_{\text{fat}}, z_{\text{sugar}})$. After scaling, a difference of one unit means "one typical spread in that ingredient", whichever ingredient it is.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scaling
# TABLE: per ingredient in p: min, max, mean (mu_i), standard deviation (sigma_i) over the corpus.
# Backs the "57 to 75%" / "0.06 to 1.5%" figures in the Scaling paragraph and gives the
# actual mu_i, sigma_i of @eq-zscore. scaler_stats(pipe) returns mu, sigma.
```

**Ingredient types.** Each type $t_i$ is one-hot encoded as $\mathbf{h}_i \in \{0,1\}^{\lvert\mathcal{T}_i\rvert}$: a 1 in the position of $t_i$ within $\mathcal{T}_i$ and 0 elsewhere. With $\mathcal{T}_{\text{flour}}$ ordered as listed above, a bread flour formula has $\mathbf{h}_{\text{flour}} = (0, 1, 0, 0, 0)$. For fat and sugar, $\text{none}$ is a level of its own, so an absent enrichment is encoded explicitly rather than as all zeros.

**Feature vector.** Stacking the standardized ratios and the type encodings gives the feature vector:

$$
\mathbf{x} = \phi(r) =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{z} \\ \mathbf{h}_{\text{flour}} \\ \mathbf{h}_{\text{yeast}} \\ \mathbf{h}_{\text{fat}} \\ \mathbf{h}_{\text{sugar}}
\end{bmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^d,
\qquad
d = 5 + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} \lvert\mathcal{T}_i\rvert
$$ {#eq-features}

```{python}

# TABLE: the same worked-example recipe as tbl-worked-example, shown as its feature vector x:
```

## Centroid Affinity Scoring

As mentioned before, we started by developing style centroids in our feature space for each class member; Sicillian, New York, and Neapolitan. We calculate a style centroid vector as the mean of each feature vector of the scaled feature set.

$$
\mathbf{c}_s = \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{D}_s\rvert} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{D}_s} \mathbf{x}^{(r)}, \qquad s \in \mathcal{S}
$$ {#eq-centroid}

Note that this does not give us a realistic formula as the values are scaled representations. Instead, this provides a baseline centroid for each style to futher compare against.

```{python}
#| label: fig-centroids
# FIGURE: viz.centroid_heatmap(pipe). Each style centroid c_s, ratio coordinates in
# standard deviations, type coordinates as shares.
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pca
# FIGURE: viz.style_scatter on the first two PCA components of x, with centroids marked
# (see fig-pca in figures.qmd). Shows how separated the styles are around their centroids.
```

We continue by calculating affinity scores for each formula in the corpus. We first measure the scaled distance from a given formula to each style centroid.

We negate and exponentiate these distances to ensure the lowest distance is represented as the highest number as a convention. 

Then, we divide by the total to standardize the distances between zero and 1. The nearest centroid will always have the highest affinity, so in this way we are using it to classify the formula.

$$
\delta_s(\mathbf{x}) = \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}_s \rVert
$$ {#eq-distance}

$$
a_s(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp\big(-\delta_s(\mathbf{x})\big)}{\sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \exp\big(-\delta_{s'}(\mathbf{x})\big)}
$$ {#eq-affinity}

We use both affinity and distance as key measures. Given a recipe, affinity measures the balance of that recipe between the three centroids. This does not describe how typical of that style the recipe is; a formula could be 100% neapolitan, but extremely far from the actual centroid. Distance then measures how close a formula is to the centroid, or how typical it is of a particular style. 


## Optimization

As describe in our motivations, many formula authors have a specific style or outcome in mind when developing a new dough recipe. This typically involves a decent amount of trial-and-error, in which other uncontrollable factors can be unintentionally introduced. Iterating in this way requires time, supplies, and introduces a degree of randomness to the outcome.

To address this, we introduce an optimization algorithm that attempts to fine-tune a formulation, given a starting formulation and target style, by minimizing the distance between input formulation and a point in formula space (e.g. a style centroid).

This may sound like a simple exercise, however we've considered two points we believe to be important to a user. Firstly, a user has a specific environment which is difficult to comprehensively measure; availability of ingredients, altitude, humidity, equipment, and so on. We assume that the user has some starting formulation they are content with, but that they would like to adjust - this initial input formulation is assumed to encode these environment variables to some degree. Under this assumption, the algorithm attempts to shrink the style distance *minimally*, such that much of the author's original recipe is perserved, while still providing new ingredient vectors that are closer to the target style. 

Secondly, users may wish to retain some ingredients that are not present in a typical style. As an example, many people will not have access to commercial flours commonly used in New York style pizza. Commercial users may advertise their use of local ingredients, including a flour with a specific protein content. A bakery with an organic live fermentation may not want to substitute with commercially produced instant yeast. Thus, the algorithm is also penalized for substituting or removing ingredients entirely.

The algorithm and loss function can be described as;

$$
\tilde{\mathbf{c}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \omega_s \mathbf{c}_s, \qquad \omega_s \ge 0, \qquad \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \omega_s = 1
$$ {#eq-target}

$$
\mathcal{E}(r) = \{ i \in \mathcal{E} : p_i > 0 \}, \qquad
\mathcal{E}_{\cap} = \mathcal{E}(r) \cap \mathcal{E}(r')
$$ {#eq-enrichments}

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(r' ; r) = {} & \lambda_{\text{target}} \lVert \mathbf{x}' - \tilde{\mathbf{c}} \rVert^2
+ \lambda_{\text{ratio}} \sum_{i \in \{\text{water}, \text{salt}, \text{yeast}\} \cup \mathcal{E}_{\cap}} \big(z'_i - z_i\big)^2 \\
& + \lambda_{\text{type}} \, \big\lvert \{ i \in \{\text{flour}, \text{yeast}\} \cup \mathcal{E}_{\cap} : t'_i \neq t_i \} \big\rvert \\
& + \lambda_{\text{remove}} \, \big\lvert \mathcal{E}(r) \setminus \mathcal{E}(r') \big\rvert
+ \lambda_{\text{add}} \, \big\lvert \mathcal{E}(r') \setminus \mathcal{E}(r) \big\rvert
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-loss}

$$
\ell_i = \min_{r \in \mathcal{D} :\, p_i^{(r)} > 0} p_i^{(r)}, \qquad
u_i = \max_{r \in \mathcal{D}} p_i^{(r)}
$$ {#eq-bounds}

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{*} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{r'} \ & L(r' ; r) \\
\text{subject to} \ & t'_i \in \mathcal{T}_i, && i \in \mathcal{K} \\
& \ell_i \le p'_i \le u_i, && i \in \{\text{water}, \text{salt}, \text{yeast}\} \cup \mathcal{E}(r') \\
& p'_i = 0, && i \in \mathcal{E} \setminus \mathcal{E}(r')
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-optimization}

$$
\operatorname{clip}_i(v) = \min\left( \max\left( v,\ \frac{\ell_i - \mu_i}{\sigma_i} \right),\ \frac{u_i - \mu_i}{\sigma_i} \right)
$$ {#eq-clip}

$$
z'_i =
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{clip}_i\left( \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{target}} \tilde{c}_i + \lambda_{\text{ratio}} z_i}{\lambda_{\text{target}} + \lambda_{\text{ratio}}} \right), & i \in \{\text{water}, \text{salt}, \text{yeast}\} \cup \mathcal{E}_{\cap} \\[2ex]
\operatorname{clip}_i\big( \tilde{c}_i \big), & i \in \mathcal{E}(r') \setminus \mathcal{E}(r) \\[1ex]
-\mu_i / \sigma_i, & i \in \mathcal{E} \setminus \mathcal{E}(r')
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ratio-solution}

$$
\mathbf{t}^{*} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{t}' \in \mathcal{T}_{\text{flour}} \times \mathcal{T}_{\text{yeast}} \times \mathcal{T}_{\text{fat}} \times \mathcal{T}_{\text{sugar}}} L\big(r'(\mathbf{t}') ; r\big)
$$ {#eq-type-search}


## Conclusion

- Do pizza dough formulations carry enough information to indicate a specific style, in absence of other recipe parameters?
- Are expert labels consistent and can a style be narrowly defined?
- Are the centroids specific enough to be informative?
- Can this information be used in dough formulation development?

## Notation {.appendix}

@tbl-notation collects the notation used in this report. Each symbol keeps one meaning throughout.

**Conventions.** Scalars are italic ($p_i$), vectors are bold lowercase ($\mathbf{p}$), and sets are calligraphic ($\mathcal{D}$). Ingredient and type names are set upright, as in $p_{\text{water}}$ or $t_{\text{flour}} = \text{bread}$. The subscript $i$ always ranges over ingredients and the subscript $s$ over styles. A parenthesized superscript names a recipe, as in $p_i^{(r)}$, and is dropped when only one recipe is being discussed. Vectors are column vectors: they are written inline as tuples and stacked vertically in displayed equations.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:--|:----------|
| $r$ | A dough formula (recipe), represented as in @eq-recipe |
| $\mathcal{D}$ | The reference corpus of curated formulas, $\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert = 32$ |
| $\mathcal{I}$ | Ingredients measured by mass: flour, water, salt, yeast, fat, sugar |
| $\mathcal{K}$ | Ingredients that also have a type: flour, yeast, fat, sugar ($\mathcal{K} \subset \mathcal{I}$) |
| $i$ | Index over ingredients |
| $m_i$ | Mass of ingredient $i$, in grams; $m_{\text{flour}}$ is the total of all flours |
| $p_i$ | Baker's percentage of ingredient $i$ (@eq-bakers) |
| $\mathbf{p}$ | Ratio vector $(p_{\text{water}}, p_{\text{salt}}, p_{\text{yeast}}, p_{\text{fat}}, p_{\text{sugar}}) \in \mathbb{R}^5_{\ge 0}$ |
| $t_i$ | Type of ingredient $i \in \mathcal{K}$ |
| $\mathcal{T}_i$ | Vocabulary of types for ingredient $i \in \mathcal{K}$; includes $\text{none}$ for fat and sugar |
| $\mu_i,\ \sigma_i$ | Mean and population standard deviation of $p_i$ over the reference recipes (@eq-zscore) |
| $z_i$ | Standardized ratio of ingredient $i$ (@eq-zscore) |
| $\mathbf{z}$ | Standardized ratio vector $(z_{\text{water}}, z_{\text{salt}}, z_{\text{yeast}}, z_{\text{fat}}, z_{\text{sugar}}) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ |
| $\mathbf{h}_i$ | One-hot encoding of $t_i$, $\in \{0,1\}^{\lvert\mathcal{T}_i\rvert}$ |
| $\phi$ | Feature map from a formula to its feature vector (@eq-features) |
| $\mathbf{x}$ | Feature vector of a formula, $\mathbf{x} = \phi(r) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ |
| $d$ | Dimension of the feature space, $5 + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} \lvert\mathcal{T}_i\rvert$ (20 for the current corpus) |
| $\mathcal{S}$ | Pizza styles: Neapolitan, New York, Sicilian |
| $s,\ s'$ | Indices over styles in $\mathcal{S}$ |
| $\mathcal{D}_s$ | Formulas in the corpus labelled with style $s$ ($\mathcal{D}_s \subset \mathcal{D}$) |
| $\mathbf{c}_s$ | Centroid of style $s$: the mean feature vector of $\mathcal{D}_s$ (@eq-centroid), $\in \mathbb{R}^d$ |
| $\delta_s(\mathbf{x})$ | Euclidean distance from feature vector $\mathbf{x}$ to centroid $\mathbf{c}_s$ (@eq-distance) |
| $a_s(\mathbf{x})$ | Affinity of feature vector $\mathbf{x}$ for style $s$ (@eq-affinity) |
| $r',\ \mathbf{x}',\ z'_i,\ p'_i,\ t'_i$ | A candidate adjustment of formula $r$, and its feature vector, standardized ratios, baker's percentages, and types |
| $r^{*}$ | The adjusted formula: the candidate that minimizes $L$ (@eq-optimization) |
| $\omega_s$ | Share of style $s$ in a target blend; $\omega_s = 1$ for a single-style target (@eq-target) |
| $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}$ | Target point in feature space, the $\omega$-weighted blend of style centroids (@eq-target), $\in \mathbb{R}^d$ |
| $\tilde{c}_i$ | Coordinate of $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}$ for the standardized ratio $z_i$ |
| $\mathcal{E}$ | Optional enrichment ingredients: fat, sugar ($\mathcal{E} \subset \mathcal{K}$) |
| $\mathcal{E}(r)$ | Enrichments present in formula $r$ (@eq-enrichments) |
| $\mathcal{E}_{\cap}$ | Enrichments present in both $r$ and $r'$ (@eq-enrichments) |
| $L(r' ; r)$ | Loss of adjusting formula $r$ to candidate $r'$ (@eq-loss) |
| $\lambda_{\text{target}},\ \lambda_{\text{ratio}},\ \lambda_{\text{type}},\ \lambda_{\text{remove}},\ \lambda_{\text{add}}$ | Loss weights for the pull toward $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}$, ratio changes, type swaps, removed enrichments, and added enrichments (@eq-loss) |
| $\ell_i,\ u_i$ | Smallest nonzero and largest observed $p_i$ over the corpus (@eq-bounds) |
| $\operatorname{clip}_i$ | Clamp of a standardized ratio to $[\ell_i, u_i]$ expressed in standard deviations (@eq-clip) |
| $\mathbf{t}',\ \mathbf{t}^{*}$ | A candidate type assignment $(t'_{\text{flour}}, t'_{\text{yeast}}, t'_{\text{fat}}, t'_{\text{sugar}})$, and the optimal one (@eq-type-search) |
| $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert$ | Euclidean norm of a vector $\mathbf{v}$ |
| $\lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert$ | Number of elements in a set $\mathcal{A}$ |
